slides.title: E/E Architecture Definition & Characteristics
slides.body:
E/E Architecture is usually defined by means of:
EE Architecture Characteristic Purpose
EEA Standards Engineering Standards - - EMC, Electrical Systems, Networks, Diagnostics, Vehicle Configuration Management,
Development Processes, ...
Network Topology Defines overall communications network within the vehicle including which ECUs are on which communication bus
and the type of power feed used for those ECUs..
SLA (Sense / Logic / Actuation) Defines distribution of feature and function including inputs and outputs
Electrical Interface Defines hardware electrical interfaces between ECUs and switches, sensors, actuators and other ECUs
Network Management
(related to AUTOSAR)
Defines networking "wake-up" and "sleep" management
Diagnostic Requirements Defines basic diagnostic specs, flash bootloader and diagnostic services and protocol
Vehicle Configuration Management Defines the methodology used to communicate vehicle specific content (standard and optional features) to the vehicle
ECUs thereby reducing module part number complexity
Network Database Defines CAN and LIN message IDs, data length, timing, and signal content and location
VF (Vehicle Functions) Detailed description of the functionality, exchanged signals, and algorithms related to a particular feature or
sub-feature
● Electrical interfaces (sensors, pedal assembly, starter)
● ECU re-programming & Vehicle Configuration
Management
● Cyber Security level / AUTOSAR compliancy

slides.title: Sleep/Wake up CAN
slides.body:
Sleep/Wake upCAN
The CAN-C1, CAN-C2 and CAN-BH networks enter Sleep mode (fall asleep) after about 10 ÷ 12
seconds from the moment the key has been turned OFF.
The networks "wake up" with the key in the OFF position when one of the car doors changes from
the "Closed" to the "Open" state.

slides.title: Key Drivers for E/E Architecture Development
slides.body:
The following items are key drivers in a Network
Architecture:
1. Integration Functions Complexity
● Complexity/magnitude of new requirements are escalating at an exponential rate
2. Bus Load Capacity
● Current architecture networks are running at 50-60% bus load (C-CAN)
● To ensure robust communication (no missed message or latency issues), networks are maintained below a threshold of 65-70% bus load
● Extrapolating the expected bus loads based on new features with new bus message requirements, the current C-CAN bus could exceed bus load limits if not
properly managed
3. Cyber Security
● Carmakers must protect its vehicles against Cyber attacks. Secure CAN communication requires message authentication (message data increases by 50% to
support message authentication)
● Safety critical modules will require hardware Trust Anchors (as many as 18 ECUs on high feature content vehicles)
4. AUTOSAR
● AUTOSAR is an open and standardized automotive SW architecture which allows SW exchangeability between vehicle platform, supplier’s solutions, OEM’s
applications
● Main benefits: Formal & Defined Architecture, Hardware Independence, Software Interfacing Standardization, Functional Safety support

slides.title: VF (Vehicle Functions)
slides.body:
VF
▪ Vehicle Functions
● Functionalities that need an interaction (usually via CAN/LIN networks) of different Electronic Control Units (ECUs) inside
a vehicle
● VFs include high level integration requirements among vehicle ECUs
● VFs are specific for each car line and for each E/E architecture

slides.title: CAN Vehicle network
Nextgen Vehicle network
slides.body:
The car is equipped with an electrical / electronic architecture called Next-Generation. Data
transmission between the various ECUs in the Next-Generation architecture takes place via
the following three digital networks:
□ CAN-C1 (high speed 500 Kb / s)
□ CAN-C2 (high speed 500 Kb / s)
□ CAN-BH (medium speed 125 Kb / s)

slides.title: CAN Private
slides.body:
CANPrivate
The ACC module is connected with a dedicated CAN-C line with the Half module. The reason for the presence of a dedicated
data transmission line between the two modules is due to the continuous exchange of information between them during the
operation of the adaptive cruise control and the FCW function.

slides.title: Port OBD-II
slides.body:
PortOBD-II
Multiple DLC Diagnosis Connector – OBD-II or EOBD
The diagnostic multiple connector pins dedicated to the three networks are:
Pin 3 - CAN-BH High
Pin 11 - CAN - BH Low
Pin 12 - CAN-C2 High
Pin13 - CAN-C2 Low
Pin 14 - CAN-C1 Low
Pin 6 - CAN-C1 High

slides.title: Test CAN
slides.body:
TestCAN
Voltage levels Digital networks. The voltage levels of the three networks can be read directly on the diagnostic connector using the
multimeter in Ohm function.

slides.title: Test CAN
slides.body:
CAN
Electrical continuity of networks.
The three digital networks CAN-C1, CAN-C2 and CAN-BH have 120Ω terminating resistors. When the network that interconnects the two
terminating resistors is electrically continuous, the value that the operator reads on the display is about 60Ω for all three networks.
